messages.body_plain:
Hey,

I assume this is because the file is binned into mz bins.

You can check your mz parameters with "dim(msset)", this gives you the number of features which is the number of mz values. Furthermore you can check the range of the mz values with "range(mz(msset))".
If you divide the mz range by the bin number you get the size of each mz bin. This is why you have small differences between the mz you want to plot and the mz of the closest bin.

In the Cardinal-walkthrough pdf you can also find how to find the mz which is closest to your mz of interest:

features(msset, mz=3000) # returns the feature number most closely matching m/z 3000
m/z = 2999.8
607

#this means bin number 607 with the mz value of 2999.8 is closest to a mz of 3000

It seems that the image function automatically uses the closest mz bin :)

For moving the display the only way I know how to change it, is by changing the y axis coordinates by adding y coordinates which are a bit wider than the y coordinates of your msset. Just add them with a comma to the image function: "ylim = c(y1,y2)"

I hope that helps you ;)
Melanie

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The image() method will use the nearest m/z value found to the one which you request.

If you used mz=322.251 and m/z 322.32 is plotted then that means that 322.32 is the closest m/z value in your dataset, and exactly 322.251 does not occur in the dataset.

You can see all of the m/z values in your dataset by using mz(object).

There was a bug in older versions that sometimes meant the wrong m/z was used (it may have used an m/z value very close to the one you requested). This was due to using a faster but sometimes imperfect lookup method, but this has since been changed in more recent versions.

If you're sure m/z 322.251 was measured in your dataset but it doesn't appear in your MSImageSet object, then the culprit is likely in the conversion to Analyze. I'm not sure what the Bruker software does during conversion, but it's entirely possible it does some binning when converting.

-Kylie

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I wrote a work-around for writing continuous imzMLs from Cardinal using MALDIquant. However, MALDIquant does not store any experiment metadata besides imaging resolution (for now), but it may help in any case. I haven't tested it with other softwares at all.

This just makes a list of MALDIquant MassSpectrum objects from the iData and mz of a Cardinal dataset which can be written into an imzML. I think you could make it to work with processed data with a few tweaks. This will work with peak picked data as well as full range mass data, but beware of memory problems if writing full range data (not sure how it will work if loading off hard disk either). If using peak picked data, other softwares will likely assume the data is full range data and you'll have ugly specs in display, but the peak data should still be good.

##install and load required packages

install.packages("MALDIquant")
install.packages("MALDIquantForeign")
require(MALDIquant)
require(MALDIquantForeign)

cardinaldata <- DAN_001.peaks

#function for writing continuous imzML from continous Cardinal data

writeImzML <- function(cardinaldata, filepath = "myimzML.imzML", processed = FALSE, pixelSize= c(100, 100)){

  #matrix of integer coordinates
  xy <- as.matrix(Cardinal::coord(cardinaldata)[,1:2])

  #mz axis of continuous dataset
  mzs <- Cardinal::mz(cardinaldata)

  #initialize list for storage of spectra
  mq <- list()

  #loop through each column of the cardinal iData and create MALDIquant objects
  for(i in 1:ncol(cardinaldata)){
    mq[[i]] <- createMassSpectrum(mass = mzs, intensity = iData(cardinaldata)[,i])
  }

  #write using MALDIquantForeign's routine
  exportImzMl(mq, path = filepath, force = TRUE, processed = processed,
              coordinates = xy, pixelSize = pixelSize)

}

Heath
